cards.front: What is a drug-drug interaction, and when is it most likely?
cards.back: Modification of one drug's response by another given together or in quick succession. The change is usually quantitative (more or less effect) and sometimes qualitative (a different or abnormal response). Risk rises with the number of drugs, so it is highest in polypharmacy.

cards.front: What is a pharmaceutical (in-vitro) interaction?
cards.back: Physical or chemical incompatibility between drugs mixed before administration, for example in one syringe or infusion bottle, leading to inactivation or precipitation. Examples: penicillin or ampicillin with an aminoglycoside, thiopentone with succinylcholine or morphine, heparin with penicillin, noradrenaline in bicarbonate solution. Avoid mixing parenteral drugs.

cards.front: Name the three categories of drug interaction.
cards.back: Pharmacokinetic: the concentration of the object drug at its site changes. Pharmacodynamic: the response changes although concentration is unchanged. Pharmaceutical: the drugs inactivate each other when mixed in vitro before administration.

cards.front: At which sites can a pharmacokinetic interaction occur?
cards.back: Absorption, protein binding, metabolism and excretion. Each alters how much active drug reaches the site of action, so effect rises or falls without any change in receptor behaviour.

cards.front: Short note: Classification of drug interactions

points: Modification of one drug's effect by another
Quantitative (more or less effect) or qualitative (abnormal response)
Changes the concentration of the object drug at its site of action
Sites: absorption, protein binding, metabolism, excretion
Changes the response at the target site, concentration unchanged
Synergism, antagonism or an abnormal response
Incompatibility before administration (same syringe or bottle)
Narrow safety margin drugs: aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium
Saturation-kinetic drugs: phenytoin, theophylline

cards.front: Classify: tetracycline plus iron, probenecid plus penicillin, penicillin plus tetracycline, and penicillin with an aminoglycoside in one syringe.
cards.back: Tetracycline-iron: pharmacokinetic (absorption, insoluble complex in gut). Probenecid-penicillin: pharmacokinetic (excretion). Penicillin-tetracycline: pharmacodynamic (bactericidal antagonized by bacteriostatic). Penicillin-aminoglycoside in one syringe: pharmaceutical (inactivation).

cards.front: Why does interaction risk rise sharply in patients on many drugs, and which drug types are most vulnerable?
cards.back: Each added drug adds possible pairs, so polypharmacy multiplies risk. Most vulnerable are drugs with a narrow safety margin (aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium), drugs controlling closely regulated functions (antihypertensives, antidiabetics, anticoagulants) and highly protein-bound or saturation-kinetics drugs.

cards.front: A patient on several drugs has lost the effect of one drug and gained toxicity from another. Reason out which interaction categories could explain each and how you would tell them apart.
cards.back: Loss of effect: reduced absorption or enterohepatic recycling, enzyme induction, increased excretion, or pharmacodynamic antagonism. Toxicity: enzyme inhibition, reduced excretion, displacement from binding, or additive pharmacodynamic effect. If drug levels move, the cause is pharmacokinetic; if levels are unchanged but response differs, it is pharmacodynamic. Pharmaceutical incompatibility applies only to drugs mixed before injection.

cards.front: Drugs prone to displacement interactions
cards.text: Highly {{protein-bound}} drugs with a small {{volume of distribution}} are most at risk, e.g. {{coumarin anticoagulants}}, {{sulfonylureas}}, certain {{NSAIDs}} and {{antiepileptics}}.

cards.front: What is enterohepatic recycling and why does it matter for interactions?
cards.back: A drug conjugated in the liver is excreted in bile, then deconjugated by gut bacteria and reabsorbed. Antibiotics such as ampicillin, tetracyclines or cotrimoxazole reduce gut flora, cut recycling and lower levels of drugs like oral contraceptive steroids.

cards.front: Why are tetracyclines poorly absorbed when taken with iron, calcium or antacids?
cards.back: They form insoluble chelate complexes in the gut lumen, so less drug is absorbed and treatment can fail. Separate the doses by 2 to 3 hours so they do not meet in the gut.

cards.front: How can broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives?
cards.back: Normal gut flora deconjugate steroid glucuronides excreted in bile, which allows enterohepatic recycling. Ampicillin, tetracyclines and cotrimoxazole reduce this flora, so less steroid is recycled and contraceptive levels fall. Advise alternative contraception.

cards.front: When does protein-binding displacement become clinically important?
cards.back: Only when the displaced drug is highly bound with a small volume of distribution, and the displacer binds the same site with higher affinity. The rise in free drug is usually brief because free drug is quickly cleared. It matters most when tissue binding is also displaced or when metabolism or excretion is inhibited, as with quinidine raising digoxin levels.

cards.front: Short note: Protein-binding displacement interactions

points: Displacer competes for the same plasma protein site with higher affinity
Free fraction of the object drug rises transiently
Highly bound, small volume of distribution
Coumarin anticoagulants, sulfonylureas, some NSAIDs, antiepileptics
Free drug is distributed, metabolised and excreted
Steady-state levels rise only marginally
Tissue binding is also displaced
Metabolism or excretion is also inhibited
Sulfonamides with phenytoin, warfarin and sulfonylureas
Quinidine with digoxin

cards.front: Compare how iron and an antibiotic course can each make a drug fail, and say how management differs.
cards.back: Iron or antacids chelate tetracycline in the gut, a local absorption block fixed by separating doses by 2 to 3 hours. A broad-spectrum antibiotic depletes gut flora and breaks enterohepatic recycling of oral contraceptive steroids, a systemic effect that spacing cannot fix, so alternative contraception is advised.

cards.front: Microsomal enzyme inducers and inhibitors
cards.text: Enzyme inducers include {{rifampicin}}, {{carbamazepine}}, {{phenytoin}} and {{phenobarbitone}}, plus chronic {{alcohol}} and {{cigarette smoking}}. Enzyme inhibitors include {{erythromycin}}, {{ketoconazole}}, {{cimetidine}} and {{ciprofloxacin}}.

cards.front: What is P-glycoprotein, and how do its inhibitors cause interactions?
cards.back: P-glycoprotein is an ATP-dependent efflux transporter that pumps drugs out of cells. Inhibitors such as quinidine reduce renal and biliary clearance of substrates like digoxin and also reduce tissue binding, so digoxin blood levels can nearly double with toxicity.

cards.front: Which drugs are metabolised by saturation kinetics and why does that make inhibition dangerous?
cards.back: Phenytoin and theophylline. Their metabolic enzymes are near saturation at usual doses, so a small drop in enzyme activity from an inhibitor produces a disproportionate rise in plasma level and toxicity.

cards.front: How do enzyme inhibition and enzyme induction differ in onset and offset?
cards.back: Inhibition develops quickly and wears off soon after the inhibitor is stopped. Induction takes about 1 to 2 weeks to reach full effect and regresses over 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal. Inhibition matters most for drugs cleared by saturation kinetics.

cards.front: Why does grapefruit juice interact with some oral drugs?
cards.back: Grapefruit juice constituents (e.g. naringin, furanocoumarins) inhibit CYP3A4, especially in the intestinal wall. Less first-pass metabolism raises the bioavailability of oral CYP3A4 substrates, so some drug labels advise avoiding grapefruit juice. Terfenadine was withdrawn partly because erythromycin or grapefruit juice blocked its CYP3A4 metabolism and the accumulated parent drug caused arrhythmias.

cards.front: Give two excretion interactions and their clinical use.
cards.back: Probenecid blocks tubular secretion of penicillins and cephalosporins and prolongs their half-life; this is used deliberately for single-dose treatment of gonorrhoea. Diuretics (and to a lesser extent tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors and some NSAIDs) raise steady-state lithium levels by increasing its tubular reabsorption; monitor lithium levels and reduce the dose.

cards.front: Short note: Renal excretion interactions

points: Mostly drugs actively secreted by renal tubular transport
Urine pH changes ionisation and excretion of weak acids and bases
Blocks secretion of penicillins and cephalosporins
Used deliberately in single-dose gonorrhoea therapy
Blocks the uricosuric action of probenecid
Reduces tubular secretion of methotrexate
Reduces secretion of canrenone, blunting spironolactone's K+-sparing action
Diuretics (including furosemide), tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors, some NSAIDs and metronidazole raise levels
Monitor level and reduce dose
Altering urine pH has been used to hasten excretion in poisoning

cards.front: A patient stable on warfarin is started on rifampicin. What happens and why?
cards.back: Rifampicin induces hepatic microsomal enzymes, so warfarin is metabolised faster and its effect is lost. Induction builds over 1 to 2 weeks and regresses over 1 to 3 weeks after stopping rifampicin, so monitor INR and adjust the dose both ways.

cards.front: Essay: Enzyme induction versus enzyme inhibition

points: Hepatic microsomal (CYP450) metabolism is the main route of many interactions
Two opposite effects: loss of effect (induction) and toxicity (inhibition)
Inhibition: competition for the same isoenzyme or cofactor, rapid onset
Induction: gene-mediated increase in enzyme synthesis, slow onset
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, smoking, chronic alcohol
Lower levels of oral contraceptives, warfarin, corticosteroids, sulfonylureas
Macrolides, azole antifungals, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, HIV protease inhibitors
Raise levels of phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, theophylline, cyclosporine
Greatest for saturation-kinetic drugs such as phenytoin and theophylline
Narrow-margin drugs need level or response monitoring
Check inducer or inhibitor status before adding or stopping a drug
Adjust dose and monitor; induction fades slowly after withdrawal

cards.front: Pharmacodynamic pairs and their effect
cards.text: Benzodiazepines with opioids cause additive {{CNS depression}} and {{respiratory depression}}; {{ACE inhibitors}} with potassium-sparing diuretics cause {{hyperkalaemia}}; propranolol with insulin can cause {{hypoglycaemia}} that is silent.

cards.front: What is the difference between synergism and antagonism in a drug interaction?
cards.back: Synergism: the combined effect is greater than from either drug alone. Antagonism: one drug blunts the effect of the other. Both occur without change in drug concentration when pharmacodynamic.

cards.front: Which drug combinations cause additive CNS depression?
cards.back: Benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, neuroleptics, opioids and alcohol in any combination. The result is excessive sedation, respiratory depression and motor incoordination.

cards.front: Why should a bactericidal beta-lactam not be combined with a bacteriostatic antibiotic?
cards.back: Bacteriostatic drugs halt bacterial growth, and the bactericidal action of penicillins and cephalosporins can be antagonized by them. Tetracycline with penicillin is the classic pair to avoid; the chapter advises against concurrent use.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacodynamic interactions in practice

points: Change in response at the target site without a change in concentration
Synergism (enhanced), antagonism (blunted) or an abnormal response
Benzodiazepine, sedating antihistamine, neuroleptic, opioid or alcohol
Sedation, respiratory depression, motor incoordination
Alpha blockers, vasodilators, ACE inhibitors, high-ceiling diuretics, cardiac depressants
Postural hypotension and fainting
Propranolol blocks recovery from hypoglycaemia and some warning symptoms
Hypoglycaemia can be silent with insulin or sulfonylureas
Levodopa blocked by neuroleptics and metoclopramide (dopamine blockade)
Macrolides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol block each other at the 50S ribosome
ACE inhibitors with potassium-sparing diuretics
Monitor potassium

cards.front: Why is sildenafil (or tadalafil) contraindicated with organic nitrates?
cards.back: Nitrates increase generation of cGMP, while sildenafil inhibits PDE5, which breaks cGMP down. Together they cause marked potentiation: a precipitous fall in BP and myocardial ischaemia. Concurrent use is contraindicated.

cards.front: Why can propranolol mask hypoglycaemia in a diabetic on insulin, and why do ACE inhibitors plus K+-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalaemia?
cards.back: Beta blockade blunts the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia and impairs recovery, so low sugar goes unnoticed. ACE inhibitors plus K+-sparing diuretics together cause severe hyperkalaemia.

cards.front: A hypertensive patient takes an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic and is given an NSAID for arthritis. Reason out the outcome.
cards.back: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, which blunts the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors and diuretics, so BP rises. Avoid concurrent use.

cards.front: Interacting pairs with theophylline and statins
cards.text: Theophylline is metabolised by {{saturation}} kinetics and has a narrow margin, so enzyme inhibitors such as {{ciprofloxacin}}, erythromycin or allopurinol can cause toxicity. Statin myopathy risk rises with fibrates such as {{gemfibrozil}}, {{niacin}}, {{erythromycin}}, {{azole antifungals}} and {{HIV protease inhibitors}}.

cards.front: Why is warfarin so prone to interactions?
cards.back: It is highly protein-bound and its effect is closely regulated (INR monitored), so displacers, metabolic inhibitors, enzyme inducers, drugs that cut gut vitamin K production, and antiplatelet drugs all shift bleeding risk.

cards.front: Which drugs raise digoxin toxicity risk when combined?
cards.back: Quinidine (reduces tissue binding and P-gp clearance, nearly doubling levels), diuretics causing hypokalaemia (give a K+-sparing diuretic or K+ supplements), and propranolol (marked bradycardia in digitalized patients).

cards.front: List the main ways other drugs raise the bleeding risk with warfarin.
cards.back: Displacement plus inhibited metabolism plus less gut vitamin K (sulfonamides, cotrimoxazole); inhibited metabolism (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, macrolides, azole antifungals, chloramphenicol, allopurinol); less vitamin K from gut flora (ampicillin, amoxicillin, sulfonamides); additive hypoprothrombinaemia (ceftriaxone, cefoperazone); added antiplatelet effect (aspirin, clopidogrel, carbenicillin). Inducers (rifampin, barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine) do the opposite and reduce warfarin effect. Monitor INR and adjust the dose.

cards.front: Which important interactions occur with aspirin and other NSAIDs?
cards.back: They reduce the effect of ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and diuretics (thiazides, furosemide) by inhibiting renal prostaglandin synthesis. They displace and/or reduce elimination of sulfonylureas, phenytoin, valproate and methotrexate (toxicity; paracetamol is the safer substitute). With warfarin or heparin they add bleeding risk (antiplatelet action plus gastric damage). With fluoroquinolones they increase CNS toxicity and seizures. With alcohol or corticosteroids they raise gastric mucosal damage and bleeding. Aspirin also blunts spironolactone by reducing tubular secretion of canrenone.

cards.front: Why do ciprofloxacin, erythromycin and allopurinol raise theophylline toxicity?
cards.back: They inhibit theophylline metabolism, and because theophylline is cleared by saturable kinetics with a narrow margin, plasma levels rise disproportionately, causing toxicity.

cards.front: Why are MAO inhibitors dangerous when combined with other drugs?
cards.back: Non-selective MAO inhibitors stop breakdown of monoamines. Tyramine-rich foods (cheese, beer, wine, yeast extract) or ephedrine-containing cold remedies release large amounts of noradrenaline: hypertensive crisis ('cheese reaction'). Interactions also occur with TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and levodopa; SSRIs combined with serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, tramadol, pethidine) can cause serotonin syndrome. Pethidine with an MAOI causes excitation, fever, convulsions and respiratory depression (excess norpethidine). CNS depressants are potentiated. Moclobemide (reversible MAO-A inhibitor) carries little tyramine risk.

points: Quinidine reduces tissue binding and P-gp-mediated renal and biliary clearance of digoxin, nearly doubling levels
Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia increases toxicity: give a K+-sparing diuretic or K+ supplement
Propranolol in digitalised patients: marked bradycardia
Serum digoxin and potassium levels
Heart rate and rhythm

Antimalarials: quinine, mefloquine, artemisinin, halofantrine
Antibacterials: sparfloxacin, moxifloxacin; antihistamines: terfenadine, astemizole, ebastine
Tricyclic antidepressants; antipsychotics (thioridazine, pimozide, aripiprazole, ziprasidone); cisapride
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia predispose to torsades
Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia raises the torsades risk with quinidine
CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) raised terfenadine, astemizole and cisapride levels, causing arrhythmias

cards.front: What are the practical steps to prevent or manage a drug interaction?
cards.back: Take a detailed history of every drug the patient is already taking, especially regular medication (antidiabetics, antihypertensives, anticoagulants, antiepileptics, oral contraceptives). Consider interactions whenever a drug is added. Stagger doses of complex-forming drugs by 2 to 3 hours. Adjust the dose and monitor levels or effects (INR, lithium, digoxin), or avoid the combination if the interaction is serious. A possible interaction does not always forbid concurrent use.

cards.front: Beneficial (deliberate) drug interactions
cards.text: ACE inhibitors with diuretics treat {{hypertension}}; {{sulfamethoxazole}} with {{trimethoprim}} is a synergistic antibacterial pair; {{furosemide}} with {{amiloride}} prevents {{hypokalaemia}}; adrenaline is added to {{lidocaine}} for local anaesthesia.

cards.front: Give deliberate drug combinations that exploit an interaction and explain why each works.
cards.back: Sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim: synergistic antibacterial pair. Adrenaline added to lidocaine: complementary action in local anaesthesia. Furosemide with amiloride: K+-sparing action offsets potassium loss.

cards.front: Probenecid is added to penicillin deliberately, but a diuretic is added to a patient on lithium. How is each handled?
cards.back: Probenecid blocks tubular secretion of penicillin and prolongs its action; used on purpose in single-dose gonorrhoea treatment. Diuretics raise lithium by promoting tubular reabsorption; tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors and certain NSAIDs do similarly, and metronidazole or tinidazole reduce its excretion. Reduce the lithium dose and monitor its level, or avoid the combination.

cards.front: Essay: Preventing and managing drug interactions in a patient on several drugs

points: Risk rises with the number of drugs, especially regular medication for chronic disease
Some combinations are deliberate and useful
Narrow safety margin: aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium
Closely regulated functions: antihypertensives, antidiabetics, anticoagulants
Highly protein-bound: NSAIDs, oral anticoagulants, sulfonylureas
Saturation kinetics: phenytoin, theophylline
Detailed drug history of all current medication
Consider interactions whenever a drug is added or stopped
Avoid mixing parenteral drugs in one syringe or bottle
Laboratory: INR, lithium, digoxin, potassium
Clinical: bleeding, bradycardia, sedation, hypotension, hypoglycaemia
Dose adjustment
Staggered administration (2-3 h gap)
Substitution, e.g. paracetamol instead of an NSAID
A possible interaction is not always a contraindication
Knowing the mechanism allows safe concurrent use with appropriate adjustments

cards.front: Why is paracetamol more dangerous in a chronic alcoholic or a patient on enzyme inducers?
cards.back: One metabolite of paracetamol causes the overdose hepatotoxicity, and induced enzymes form more of it, so the toxic dose is lower. In chronic alcoholism doses below 3 g/day are considered safe.

cards.front: Why must neuroleptics and metoclopramide be avoided in a patient on levodopa-carbidopa?
cards.back: Both block dopamine receptors, so they antagonise the antiparkinsonian effect of levodopa; concurrent use is contraindicated. Separately, levodopa with antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, vasodilators, prazosin) causes excessive postural hypotension, so reduce the antihypertensive dose.

cards.front: Which drugs reduce absorption of ketoconazole and of phenytoin, and by what mechanism?
cards.back: Ketoconazole needs gastric acid to dissolve, so H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors lower its absorption. Sucralfate binds phenytoin in the gut lumen, so less is absorbed.

cards.front: What reaction can occur when a patient on metronidazole (or tinidazole, cefoperazone) drinks alcohol, and what is the advice?
cards.back: Disulfiram-like or bizarre distressing symptoms in some individuals; the chapter suggests acetaldehyde accumulation, though the mechanism is not known. Warn the patient not to drink alcohol.

cards.front: What interactions does allopurinol have with ampicillin, 6-mercaptopurine/azathioprine and warfarin or theophylline?
cards.back: With ampicillin: more skin rashes (mechanism unexplained), so avoid. It inhibits metabolism of 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine, so reduce their dose to one-third. It inhibits metabolism of warfarin and theophylline: monitor and reduce the dose of the object drug.

cards.front: Name pharmacodynamic interactions of TCAs with adrenaline in local anaesthetic, and of furosemide with aminoglycosides.
cards.back: TCAs block neuronal uptake of adrenaline, potentiating it and raising BP, so use plain local anaesthetic solution. Furosemide with aminoglycosides gives additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, so avoid the pair.

cards.front: Why does propranolol prolong lidocaine action?
cards.back: Lidocaine metabolism depends on hepatic blood flow; propranolol reduces liver blood flow, so lidocaine half-life lengthens. Hence the ceiling amount of lidocaine used in local anaesthesia is reduced.

cards.front: Name the regular-medication drug classes the chapter flags as likely to be involved in interactions.
cards.back: Antidiabetics, antihypertensives, antianginals, antiarthritic drugs, antiepileptics, antiparkinsonian drugs, oral contraceptives, anticoagulants, antiasthmatics, psychopharmacological agents, antiulcer/reflux drugs, corticosteroids, antitubercular and anti-HIV drugs. Patients on these are on long-term therapy, so any newly added drug meets them.

cards.front: Why must carbenicillin or ticarcillin be avoided in a patient on aspirin or another antiplatelet drug?
cards.back: They perturb platelet surface receptors, adding to the platelet inhibition of aspirin, so bleeding risk rises. This is a pharmacodynamic additive effect, not a change in drug level; avoid the combination.

cards.front: Why should erythromycin and clindamycin (or chloramphenicol) not be combined?
cards.back: They bind to nearby sites on the bacterial 50S ribosome and interfere with each other, giving mutual antagonism of antibacterial action. Avoid concurrent use.

cards.front: How do cimetidine or isoniazid change the effect of diazepam, and what is advised?
cards.back: They inhibit diazepam metabolism, so levels rise and CNS depression is exaggerated. Avoid the pair or reduce the benzodiazepine dose.
